Summary adjusted using the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS):

- Policy stance: The FOMC keeps the federal funds rate at 0–0.25% and adopts outcome-based forward guidance under average inflation targeting. It will continue increasing Treasury and agency MBS holdings and stands ready to use repo/ON RRP to support market functioning.

- SLOOS crosswalk: The July 2020 SLOOS (covering Q2) reports broad-based tightening of lending standards and terms for businesses (C&I to firms of all sizes; CRE across categories) and households (credit cards, auto, other consumer; many residential mortgage categories). Banks raised spreads, tightened covenants, increased collateral requirements, and reduced credit line sizes. On net, demand weakened for C&I and CRE loans and for most consumer credit, while residential mortgage demand strengthened (boosted by low rates and refinancing). Banks cited a weaker economic outlook, reduced risk tolerance, and concerns in virus-sensitive sectors (e.g., energy, travel, leisure) and expected deterioration in credit quality over the coming year.

- Risks and transmission: Despite improved market functioning and supportive policy, tighter bank lending standards and weaker business/consumer loan demand point to restrained credit intermediation, especially in C&I, CRE, and consumer credit. This supports the FOMC’s caution that the outlook depends on the virus and that risks remain considerable, and it argues for sustained accommodation. Strength in housing is a meaningful but partial offset.

- Net read: The commitment to AIT and ongoing purchases is supportive, but SLOOS evidence of broad tightening and expected credit quality deterioration tilts the balance more negative than a policy-only reading; housing resilience tempers the downside.

Bottom line: Moderately negative tone given tightening credit supply and weak loan demand in key segments, partially offset by strong mortgage demand and credible Fed support.
